pumac-2018-team-01.title: Gaps are exchangeable
pumac-2018-team-01.body:
Put $a_0=0$ and $a_{1001}=2019$ and let $b_i=a_i-a_{i-1}\ge1$ for $i=1,\dots,1001$. Subsets correspond bijectively to sequences of $1001$ positive integers $(b_i)$ with sum $2019$, and the uniform distribution on subsets is the uniform distribution on such sequences, which is symmetric in the $b_i$. So all $b_i$ have the same expectation $\frac{2019}{1001}$, and
$$E[a_7]=E[b_1+\dots+b_7]=7\cdot\frac{2019}{1001}=\frac{2019}{143}.$$
This is in lowest terms ($2019=3\cdot673$, $143=11\cdot13$), so $m+n=2019+143=2162$.

**Answer: 2162**

pumac-2018-team-02.title: Coordinates
pumac-2018-team-02.body:
Let $a=BC$, $b=CA=66$, $c=AB=90$, with $B=(0,0)$, $C=(a,0)$. Then $A_x=\frac{c^2-b^2+a^2}{2a}=\frac{3744+a^2}{2a}$. The incenter has $I_x=\frac{aA_x+b\cdot0+c\cdot a}{a+b+c}=\frac{\frac{3744+a^2}2+90a}{a+156}$ and the centroid has $G_x=\frac{A_x+a}3=\frac{1248+a^2}{2a}$. $IG\perp BC$ means $I_x=G_x$:
$$\frac{3744+a^2+180a}{2(a+156)}=\frac{1248+a^2}{2a}\ \Longrightarrow\ a(3744+a^2+180a)=(a+156)(1248+a^2).$$
Expanding, $24a^2+2496a-194688=0$, i.e. $a^2+104a-8112=0$, so $a=\frac{-104+\sqrt{43264}}2=\frac{-104+208}2=52$.

**Answer: 52**

pumac-2018-team-02.title: Synthetic
pumac-2018-team-02.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, $D$ the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ (and $G$) to $BC$, and $H$ the foot of the altitude from $A$. The incircle touches $BC$ at $D$ with $BD-DC=AB-AC=24$, so with $BM=x$ we get $MD=12$. Since $G$ divides $AM$ in ratio $2:1$ and $GD\parallel AH$, $MH=3\,MD=36$. Then $BH=x+36$, $CH=|x-36|$ and $BH^2-CH^2=AB^2-AC^2=3744$ gives $144x=3744$, $x=26$ and $BC=52$.

**Answer: 52**

pumac-2018-team-03.title: Reciprocals
pumac-2018-team-03.body:
Divide numerator and denominator by $\log_35\log_25$: the expression is $\dfrac1{\frac1{\log_25}+\frac1{\log_35}}=\dfrac1{\log_52+\log_53}=\dfrac1{\log_56}=\log_65$.

So $a\log_bc=\log_bc^a=\log_65$. By unique factorization $b$ must be a power of $6$ and $c^a$ the same power of $5$, so $b\ge6$ and $a+b\ge7$, with equality exactly for $a=1$, $b=6$, $c=5$. Thus $a+2b+3c=1+12+15=28$.

**Answer: 28**

pumac-2018-team-04.title: Quadratic residues and CRT
pumac-2018-team-04.body:
Let the common remainder be $r$; it is a remainder mod $7$, so $0\le r\le6$, and $r$ must be a square mod each of $7,11,13$. Squares mod $7$: $0,1,2,4$; mod $11$: $0,1,3,4,5,9$; mod $13$: $0,1,3,4,9,10,12$. So $r\in\{0,1,4\}$ (the value $2$ is not a square mod $11$).
- $r=0$: $n\equiv0$ mod each of $7,11,13$: $1$ residue mod $1001$.
- $r=1$: $n\equiv\pm1$ mod each prime (signs independent): $8$ residues mod $1001$.
- $r=4$: $n\equiv\pm2$ mod each prime: $8$ residues.

So $17$ residues mod $1001=7\cdot11\cdot13$ work, giving $2\cdot17=34$ values among $1,\dots,2002$. For $2003\le n\le2017$ ($n\equiv1,\dots,15\pmod{1001}$) one checks that only $n\equiv1$ and $n\equiv2$ work ($2003$ and $2004$). Total $34+2=36$.

**Answer: 36**

pumac-2018-team-05.title: Match the summands
pumac-2018-team-05.body:
Subtracting the identities for $n$ and $n-1$ shows the summand at $i=n-1$ equals $\sqrt n-\sqrt{n-1}$; so for all $i\ge0$
$$\sqrt{Q(i)+1}-\sqrt{Q(i)}=\left(\sqrt{i+1}-\sqrt i\right)^5,\qquad Q(i)=ai^5+bi^4+ci^3+di^2+ei.$$
Let $s=\sqrt{i+1}$, $t=\sqrt i$. Expanding with $s^2=i+1$, $t^2=i$:
$$(s-t)^5=s\,(16i^2+12i+1)-t\,(16i^2+20i+5).$$
Since $(s-t)(s+t)=1$ we also have $\sqrt{Q+1}+\sqrt Q=(s+t)^5=s(16i^2+12i+1)+t(16i^2+20i+5)$. Adding and subtracting: $\sqrt Q=t(16i^2+20i+5)$, so
$$Q(i)=i(16i^2+20i+5)^2=256i^5+640i^4+560i^3+200i^2+25i.$$
Hence $a+b+c+d=256+640+560+200=1656$ (equivalently $Q(1)-e=41^2-25$).

**Answer: 1656**

pumac-2018-team-06.title: n is a cube
pumac-2018-team-06.body:
Let $k=\tau(n)$, so $n=k^3$ and $k=\tau(k^3)$. If $k=\prod p_i^{a_i}$ then $\tau(k^3)=\prod(3a_i+1)$, so we need
$$\prod p_i^{a_i}=\prod(3a_i+1).$$
Every factor $3a+1\equiv1\pmod3$, so $3\nmid k$. Compare ratios $\rho(p,a)=\frac{p^a}{3a+1}$: for $p=2$ they are $\frac12,\frac47,\frac45$ for $a=1,2,3$ and $>1$ for $a\ge4$; for primes $p\ge5$ every ratio is at least $\frac54$ ($5^1$: $\frac54$, $7^1$: $\frac74$, $p^a$ with $a\ge2$: at least $\frac{25}7$).

The product of all ratios must be $1$. If $2\nmid k$ then all ratios of primes $\ge5$ are $>1$, so $k=1$ ($n=1$). Otherwise the ratio $\rho_2$ of the prime $2$ must be below $1$: $a_2\in\{1,2,3\}$ and the primes $\ge5$ must have ratio-product $Q=1/\rho_2\in\{2,\frac74,\frac54\}$:
- $a_2=3$, $Q=\frac54$: exactly one prime $\ge5$ with ratio $\frac54$, namely $5^1$. So $k=2^3\cdot5=40$.
- $a_2=2$, $Q=\frac74$: a single prime with ratio $\frac74$ is $7^1$ (two primes give at least $\frac54\cdot\frac74$). So $k=2^2\cdot7=28$.
- $a_2=1$, $Q=2$: a single prime power would need $p^a=2(3a+1)$, which for $a=1$ gives $8$ (not prime) and for $a\ge2$ is impossible since then the ratio is at least $\frac{25}7>2$; two or more primes give a product of ratios at least $\frac54\cdot\frac74=\frac{35}{16}>2$. So there is no solution.

So $k\in\{1,28,40\}$, $n\in\{1,28^3,40^3\}=\{1,21952,64000\}$, and the sum is $1+21952+64000=85953$.

**Answer: 85953**

pumac-2018-team-07.title: Menelaus and AM-GM
pumac-2018-team-07.body:
Let $a=MN=13$, $b=NP=89$, $c=PM=100$. Write $I=S+\frac x2\overrightarrow{MN}$, $J=R+\frac y2\overrightarrow{NP}$, $A=B+\frac z2\overrightarrow{PM}$ ($x,y,z$ real). Then $\frac{MI}{IN}=\frac{1+x}{1-x}$, and similarly for the other two sides, so Menelaus ($I,J,A$ collinear) gives $(1+x)(1+y)(1+z)=-(1-x)(1-y)(1-z)$, i.e.
$$xy+yz+zx=-1.$$
The quantity is $\Sigma=SI+RJ+BA=\frac12(a|x|+b|y|+c|z|)$.

The three products $xy,yz,zx$ cannot all be negative (their product $(xyz)^2$ is positive), so one is $\ge0$, say $yz\ge0$. Then $xy+xz=-1-yz\le-1$, so $|x|(|y|+|z|)\ge1$. By AM-GM,
$$\Sigma\ge\tfrac12\left(a|x|+\min(b,c)(|y|+|z|)\right)\ge\sqrt{a\min(b,c)\,|x|(|y|+|z|)}\ge\sqrt{13\cdot89}.$$
Similarly, if $zx\ge0$ then $|y|(|x|+|z|)\ge1$ and $\Sigma\ge\sqrt{89\cdot\min(13,100)}=\sqrt{89\cdot13}$, and if $xy\ge0$ then $|z|(|x|+|y|)\ge1$ and $\Sigma\ge\sqrt{100\cdot13}$. All three bounds are at least $\sqrt{1157}$, so $\Sigma^2\ge1157$.

Equality: take $\ell$ through $B$ ($z=0$), so $xy=-1$, with $13|x|=89|y|$, i.e. $|x|=\sqrt{89/13}$. Then $\Sigma=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt{13\cdot89}=\sqrt{1157}$.

**Answer: 1157**

pumac-2018-team-08.title: Upper bound and construction
pumac-2018-team-08.body:
*At most 20.* With $21$ or more coins there are at most $4$ empty squares, so at most $4$ of the $5$ rows contain an empty square and some row is completely full: five coins in a row, not allowed.

*Twenty is possible.* Leave empty the five squares (row, column) $=(1,2),(2,4),(3,3),(4,1),(5,5)$: one per row and one per column, so no row or column is full, and the center square $(3,3)$ lies on both main diagonals, so neither is full.

**Answer: 20**

pumac-2018-team-09.title: Digit sums and slack
pumac-2018-team-09.body:
A number is congruent to its digit sum mod $9$. If every number has digit sum $s$, then $17s\equiv2018\equiv2\pmod 9$, so $8s\equiv2$ and $s\equiv7\pmod9$: $s=7,16,\dots$.

*$s\ge16$ is impossible:* the $17$ smallest numbers with digit sum $16$ start $79,88,97,169,178,187,196,259,\dots$, and already the first $12$ of them add up to more than $2018$.

*$s=7$:* the numbers with digit sum $7$ in order are $7,16,25,34,43,52,61,70,106,115,124,133,142,151,160,205,214,223,\dots$. The $16$ smallest sum to $1444$, so any set containing the largest element $M$ has $M\le2018-1444=574$. The largest number $\le574$ with digit sum $7$ is $520$ (the candidates $5xy$ are $502,511,520$). A set containing $520$ needs $16$ other such numbers (all below $520$) with sum $1498=1444+54$. Replacing the $k$-th smallest elements by larger ones raises the sum; replacing one of the first $16$ numbers $e$ by a larger unused number $r$ raises the sum by $r-e$, and $r-e=54$ with $e\le205$ forces $(r,e)=(214,160)$ (for $r=223,232,241,250,\dots$ the value $r-54$ is not in the list); replacing two or more numbers raises the sum by at least $214+223-(160+205)=72>54$. So the unique set is $\{7,16,25,34,43,52,61,70,106,115,124,133,142,151,205,214,520\}$ (sum $2018$).

Thus $M=520$ and there is exactly one set, so the answer is $520+1=521$.

**Answer: 521**

pumac-2018-team-10.title: Divide by abcd
pumac-2018-team-10.body:
Dividing by $abcd$: $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c=\dfrac1d+1$.
- If $a\ge3$ the left side is at most $1<1+\frac1d$. So $a=2$ and $\frac1b+\frac1c=\frac12+\frac1d$.
- If $b\ge4$ the left side is at most $\frac12<\frac12+\frac1d$. So $b\in\{2,3\}$.
- $b=2$: $\frac1c=\frac1d$, so $c=d$ with $2\le c\le418$: $417$ solutions.
- $b=3$: $\frac1c=\frac16+\frac1d$, so $c<6$ and $d=\frac{6c}{6-c}$: $c=3,4,5$ give $d=6,12,30$ (all $\le418$): $3$ solutions.

Total $417+3=420$.

**Answer: 420**

pumac-2018-team-11.title: Bounding b/a
pumac-2018-team-11.body:
We need $0.527\le\frac ab<0.528$, i.e. $\frac{1000}{528}<\frac ba\le\frac{1000}{527}$, i.e. $1.8939\ldots<\frac ba\le1.8975\ldots$. Let $k=2a-b$; then $0.1025\ldots\le\frac ka<0.1060\ldots$, i.e. $9.43\ldots<\frac ak\le9.75\ldots$.
- $k=1$: no integer $a$ in $(9.43,9.76]$.
- $k=2$: $a\in(18.86,19.52]$, so $a=19$, $b=2\cdot19-2=36$, and indeed $\frac{19}{36}=0.52777\ldots$.
- $k\ge3$ needs $a>28.3$, so $a\ge29$ and $a+b>29+54=83$.

For $a\le18$ only $k=1$ could work (since $\frac ka\ge0.1025$ forces $k\ge1$, and $k\ge2$ needs $a\ge19$), but $k=1$ has no solution. For $a\ge20$, $b>1.8939\cdot20>37.8$, so $a+b\ge58>55$. Hence the minimum is $19+36=55$.

**Answer: 55**

pumac-2018-team-12.title: Ceva and mass points
pumac-2018-team-12.body:
The right angle is at $C$. $ZY\parallel AB$ and $ZY=4$, so $\triangle CZY\sim\triangle CAB$ with ratio $\frac4{60}=\frac1{15}$: $CY:YB=1:14$ and $CZ:ZA=1:14$.

By Ceva, with $M$ the midpoint of $AB$: $\frac{AM}{MB}\cdot\frac{BY}{YC}\cdot\frac{CZ}{ZA}=1\cdot14\cdot\frac1{14}=1$, so $AY$, $BZ$ and the median $CM$ are concurrent: $P\in CM$. Place masses $1$ at $A$, $1$ at $B$ and $14$ at $C$ (these balance $Y$ on $BC$ and $Z$ on $CA$); then $P$ is the center of mass and $CP:PM=2:14$, so $CP=\frac18CM$.

Since $C$ is the right angle, $CM=\frac{AB}2=30$, so $CP=\frac{30}8=\frac{15}4$. The centroid has $CG=\frac23CM=20$. Hence $PG=20-\frac{15}4=\frac{65}4$ and $a+b=65+4=69$.

(Coordinates confirm this: with legs $a,b$ satisfying $a^2+b^2=3600$, $ab=\frac{1800}7$, the intersection point $P$ is at distance $16.25$ from $G$.)

**Answer: 69**

pumac-2018-team-13.title: Track the red cube and the empty space
pumac-2018-team-13.body:
Only the positions of the red cube and the empty space matter. The red cube must make $90$ net unit steps (from $(0,\dots,0)$ to $(9,\dots,9)$), so at least $90$ moves of the red cube, each of which is a move in which the empty space is adjacent to red and swaps with it.

*Lower bound.* The empty space starts at distance $90$ from red, and it must reach a neighbour of red ($89$ moves of the empty space), then swap with red (move $90$). After a swap the empty space sits right behind red, at relative position $-e_i$. For red to move forward again in direction $e_j$ the empty space must be at $+e_j$ relative to red, at distance $2$ from $-e_i$, so at least $2$ empty-space moves are needed and then the swap: at least $3$ moves per further red step. With at least $90$ red steps, the total is at least $90+89\cdot3=357$.

*Construction.* Move red in the directions $1,2,\dots,10,1,2,\dots$ (each $9$ times, consecutive directions different, so red is always able to step in the next direction). After a step in direction $i$ the empty space is at $-e_i$; to be ready for direction $j\ne i$ it goes $-e_i\to-e_i+e_j\to e_j$ (two moves, inside the cube since red just moved forward in direction $i$ and still has room in direction $j$), and then swaps with red. The first red step takes $89+1=90$ moves (the empty space first walks to $e_1$ without passing through the red cube). Total $90+89\cdot3=357$.

(Brute-force searches of the same puzzle in dimensions $2$ and $3$ and side lengths $3,4$ give exactly $D+3(D-1)$ with $D$ the distance, e.g. $13$ for $3\times3$.)

**Answer: 357**

pumac-2018-team-14.title: Casework on the cube-root floor
pumac-2018-team-14.body:
For $x\ge1$, $\sqrt[3]x\ge\sqrt[4]x$, so $\lfloor\sqrt[3]x\rfloor\ge\lfloor\sqrt[4]x\rfloor$ and the possibilities are $(4,0),(3,1),(2,2)$.
- $(4,0)$: $x\ge64$ but $\lfloor\sqrt[4]x\rfloor=0$ needs $x<1$: no.
- $(3,1)$: $x\ge27$ but $\lfloor\sqrt[4]x\rfloor=1$ needs $x<16$: no.
- $(2,2)$: $8\le x<27$ and $16\le x<81$, i.e. $16\le x\le26$.

The sum is $16+17+\dots+26=\frac{11(16+26)}2=231$.

**Answer: 231**

pumac-2018-team-15.title: Unfold the cube
pumac-2018-team-15.body:
Fred's path is a space diagonal, length $2\sqrt3$, so he needs $2$ seconds. Aaron arrives first iff his surface distance to the target vertex $V$ is less than $2\sqrt2$.

*The three faces containing $V$:* every point of such a face is within $2\sqrt2$ (the face diagonal) of $V$ along the face, so all of them qualify: area $3\cdot4=12$.

*Each of the three faces not containing $V$.* Take $V=(0,0,0)$ and the face $z=2$ with coordinates $(x,y)\in[0,2]^2$. A shortest path to $V$ runs through the face $x=0$ or the face $y=0$ (both contain $V$); unfolding the face $z=2$ onto either gives the distances $\sqrt{y^2+(2+x)^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2+(2+y)^2}$ to $V$ (paths through other faces are longer). The reachable region is the union of the two disk-sections
$$D_1:\ y^2+(2+x)^2<8,\qquad D_2:\ x^2+(2+y)^2<8$$
inside the square. Each has area $\int_2^{2\sqrt2}\sqrt{8-t^2}\,dt=\pi-2$. Their intersection (symmetric about $y=x$, meeting at $x=y=\sqrt3-1$) has area
$$\int_0^{\sqrt3-1}\left(\sqrt{8-x^2}-2\right)dx+\int_{\sqrt3-1}^{2\sqrt2-2}\sqrt{8-(2+x)^2}\,dx=\Bigl(\tfrac\pi3+3-2\sqrt3\Bigr)+\Bigl(\tfrac\pi3-1\Bigr)=\tfrac{2\pi}3+2-2\sqrt3.$$
So the area on one far face is $2(\pi-2)-\left(\frac{2\pi}3+2-2\sqrt3\right)=\frac{4\pi}3+2\sqrt3-6$.

*Total:* $12+3\left(\frac{4\pi}3+2\sqrt3-6\right)=4\pi+6\sqrt3-6=4\pi+\sqrt{108}-6$, so $a+b+c=4+108-6=106$.

(A Monte Carlo estimate of the region on a far face gives $\approx1.655$, matching $\frac{4\pi}3+2\sqrt3-6\approx1.653$.)

**Answer: 106**

pumac-2018-team-16.title: Powers of two fill every residue
pumac-2018-team-16.body:
The subsets of $\{1,2,4,\dots,1024\}$ (eleven powers of two) have sums $0,1,\dots,2047$, each exactly once (binary representation), so they hit every residue mod $2048$ exactly once. Hence for every subset of the other $2018-11=2007$ numbers there is exactly one subset of the powers of two that makes the total $\equiv2018\pmod{2048}$. So $N=2^{2007}$.

Modulo $1000$: $2^{2007}\equiv0\pmod 8$, and mod $125$, $2^{100}\equiv1$ (Euler), so $2^{2007}=(2^{100})^{20}\cdot2^7\equiv128\equiv3\pmod{125}$. The number $x=128$ satisfies $x\equiv0\pmod8$ and $x\equiv3\pmod{125}$, so $N\equiv128\pmod{1000}$.

**Answer: 128**
